Clean cel-shaded anime game illustration with a touch of realism, like polished official background art in a Japanese action game: semi-realistic forms, proportions, lighting and materials; crisp, well-defined ink outlines of confident even weight around every object, with clean hard edges and clear separation between pieces; large areas of smooth colour with two- or three-tone cel shading and a few soft gradients; sharp white gloss highlights on metal; bright, slightly richer colours. Rules: smooth, clean surfaces with crisp, well-defined outlines — no grain, noise, hatching, stippling, paper or crackle texture anywhere. Draw only what the scene names. Sizes, quantities and proportions exactly as described and realistic: real commercial gym machines at true scale, with plain weight stacks and no numbers, logos or brand names anywhere.

Scene: A quiet, clean corner of a small modern gym in soft warm morning light, seen at eye level from a gentle three-quarter angle: on the left a seated chest press machine (upright cream back pad, two horizontal handles on lever arms, a plain weight stack), in the middle a tall dual-pulley cable station with two weight stacks and a stirrup handle hanging from each pulley, on the right a lat pulldown station (tall frame, high pulley, a long bar on the cable, a seat with padded knee rollers, a weight stack); dark graphite frames, cream pads, light grey plates; a small pale-wood bench with a folded terracotta-orange towel on it; a warm grey rubber floor; a pale wall with one large window letting in warm ivory daylight that casts long soft shadows. Uncluttered, tidy and inviting. No people, no mirrors with reflections, no posters, nothing written anywhere: the weight stacks are plain plates without numbers, and there are no logos or brand names.

Clean technical instruction illustration for a gym exercise guide, in the hand-drawn Japanese-animation look of the rest of the site: thin, even, warm dark-brown ink outlines (#4a3a2a) around every shape; large areas of smooth flat colour with simple matte two-tone cel shading (one base tone plus one darker shadow tone per surface — no gradients, no gloss, no texture); a plain warm ivory background (#faf6ef) filling the whole picture edge to edge, with no walls, no windows, no scenery and no props beyond what the scene names; each machine (or the mannequin's feet) stands on one soft flat shadow ellipse, nothing else marks the ground. Palette: the mannequin is a neutral matte warm grey (#d8cfc3 base, #b9ad9e shadow); machine frames are dark graphite (#3b3632); seats and pads are cream (#efe6d6); weight stacks, cables, pulleys, bars, handles, dumbbells and plates are light grey (#c9c3b8); the ONLY saturated colour in the picture is the accent orange (#b83d0b). Proportions true to real commercial gym equipment and a real adult body. Calm, tidy, diagrammatic — like the best page of a good instruction manual.

The person is a smooth stylised mannequin, gender-neutral with an athletic adult build (like a smooth artist's figure or a matte crash-test dummy): a smooth egg-shaped head with no face, no hair and no ears; simple mitten hands without individual fingers that visibly wrap around whatever they hold; smooth rounded joints; no clothing, no shoes, no muscle striations — one continuous matte grey surface, so that anatomy errors are impossible. The working muscles are painted directly on the mannequin's surface as clean flat orange (#b83d0b) regions with the same thin brown outline, shaped like the real muscle and exactly where it lies, only where the camera can see it; assisting muscles are a paler orange tint (#e8a37a). Everything else on the mannequin stays grey.

Layout: ONE landscape picture (3:2), a single scene with no panels and no dividing lines: the mannequin on the machine frozen at the hardest point of one repetition, seen from the camera the scene names (usually a pure side profile, exactly perpendicular to the movement), large and centred, so that the angles at the shoulder, elbow, hip and knee read at a glance. Draw the limbs as clean, clearly separated segments with visible joint bends, and show exactly where the mannequin touches the seat, pads and handles. Exactly ONE curved orange arrow (#b83d0b) with a simple triangular head, beside the moving hands (or the moving body part the scene names), shows the direction they travel next in the lift. No other arrows, angle marks, arcs, dots or lines.

Scene: Exercise: Seated chest press machine, done on a seated pin-loaded chest press: an upright padded back rest, an adjustable seat, two lever arms (one on each side of the seat, pivoting high on the frame behind the shoulders) that each end in a horizontal handle beside the chest and swing forward with the hands, and a weight stack with a selector pin standing behind the seat; nothing crosses in front of the chest. Camera: pure side (profile) view: the camera looks at the mannequin's left side at exactly 90 degrees to the direction it faces, so the mannequin is seen in profile facing the right side of the picture, with one arm and one leg in front and the other mostly hidden behind them; never a front, back or three-quarter view. Setup: seat height set so the handles are level with the middle of the chest; feet flat on the floor; hips, upper back and head against the back pad; a full grip on the horizontal handles with straight wrists. The one moment shown, the hardest point of the repetition: the bottom of the press: handles beside the middle of the chest, elbows bent about 90 degrees and just below shoulder height, upper arms level with the back pad, chest up, back and head on the pad. The single orange arrow follows the lifting path through this moment: from the handles beside the chest straight forward to arm's length (when this moment is the end of the lift, the arrow leads up to the hands from where they came). Paint flat orange (working muscles): the mid chest: the large fan-shaped pectoralis major from the breastbone to the front of the armpit; the upper chest: the top part of the pectoralis major just below the collarbone. Paint pale orange (assisting muscles): the front deltoid: the front of the shoulder; the triceps lateral head: the outer back of the upper arm.

The person is a smooth stylised mannequin, gender-neutral with an athletic adult build (like a smooth artist's figure or a matte crash-test dummy): a smooth egg-shaped head with no face, no hair and no ears; simple mitten hands without individual fingers that visibly wrap around whatever they hold; smooth rounded joints; no clothing, no shoes, no muscle striations — one continuous matte grey surface, so that anatomy errors are impossible. The working muscles are painted directly on the mannequin's surface as clean flat orange (#b83d0b) regions with the same thin brown outline, shaped like the real muscle and exactly where it lies, only where the camera can see it; assisting muscles are a paler orange tint (#e8a37a). Everything else on the mannequin stays grey.

Layout: ONE landscape picture (3:2), a single scene with no panels and no dividing lines: the mannequin on the machine frozen at the hardest point of one repetition, large and centred, seen from the camera the scene names. Unless the scene names another view, this is a strict PROFILE drawing, like an engineering side elevation: the camera looks at the mannequin's left side at exactly 90 degrees, the mannequin faces the right edge of the picture, only its left arm and left leg are fully visible (the right ones are hidden behind them), the head is a profile silhouette, and the flat machine parts that face forward — back pad, seat, frame — are seen edge-on as thin slabs. The angles at the shoulder, elbow, hip and knee must read at a glance: draw the limbs as clean, clearly separated segments with visible joint bends, and show exactly where the mannequin touches the seat, pads and handles. Exactly ONE curved orange arrow (#b83d0b) with a simple triangular head, beside the moving hands (or the moving body part the scene names), shows the direction of the lift through this moment. No other arrows, angle marks, arcs, dots or lines.

Scene: Exercise: Pec deck (machine fly), done on a seated pin-loaded pec deck (butterfly) machine: an upright back pad, an adjustable seat, two long swinging arms with vertical handles that swing together in front of the chest, a weight stack behind the seat. Camera: high front view: the camera in front of the seated mannequin and well above it, looking down at about 60 degrees, so both the height of the arms and how far they open behind the chest read clearly. Setup: seat set so the handles are at mid-chest height and the shoulders level with the arms' pivots; back and head against the pad; hands on the vertical handles, elbows softly bent. The exercise page describes the set-up as: Set the seat so the handles (or arm pads) are at chest height with the upper arms about parallel to the floor. Set the start position so that at the widest point your hands are level with your body, never behind it (draw consistently with it). Technique the drawing must respect (never write these as text): Head and back on the pad, shoulder blades pulled back and down; Soft, fixed bend in the elbows — the movement happens at the shoulder; Bring the handles together in a wide arc, as if hugging a big tree; Squeeze for 1 s with the hands in front of your chest, breathing out. The one moment shown, the hardest point of the repetition: the open, stretched position: upper arms at chest height and in line with the back pad (not behind it), elbows softly bent about 20 degrees, chest up, back and head on the pad. The single orange arrow follows the lifting path through this moment: an inward horizontal arc at chest height from the open position to in front of the chest (when this moment is the end of the lift, the arrow leads up to the hands from where they came). Paint flat orange (working muscles): the mid chest: the large fan-shaped pectoralis major from the breastbone to the front of the armpit. Paint pale orange (assisting muscles): the upper chest: the top part of the pectoralis major just below the collarbone; the lower chest: the lowest band of the pectoralis major along the bottom edge of the chest; the front deltoid: the front of the shoulder.
